title: CVE-2022-35252: control code in cookie denial of service
excerpt:
## Summary:
I took a look at https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/9048/commits/d7bcbc7d8d4b6d972d3da12d54819169a19c287b (a sneak peek on a vulnerability to be announced tomorrow). My guess for that vulnerability is that since cookies are persistent, someone who can trick curl into storing cookies can store large amounts of cookies into curl cookie store, which will prevent curl from ever interacting with the server (due to large request being generated causing a 400 error)

I found a separate way to do this, curl does not implement character check on cookie name or value when saving to cookie store. So for example a form feed '\f' can be saved in curl's cookie store. When form feed is sent by curl to a server such as Apache, Apache will respond with 400 Error (historically, Apache would accept, however now due to HTTP smuggling concerns, Apache will now strictly reject any such control characters.), preventing someone from ever interacting the server with the cookie store.

According to the spec, cookies should not contain control characters anyway, see https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265#section-4.1.1.

## Steps To Reproduce:

1. 

In test.php,
`````
<?php
echo("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nDate: Fri, 29 Apr 2022 10:11:55 GMT\r\nServer: Apache/2.4.43 (Debian)\r\nSet-Cookie: a=b\f; \r\nContent-Length: 0\r\nConnection: close\r\nContent-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8\r\n\r\n");
`````
Setup malicious server,
`````
php test.php | nc -nvlp 3333
`````

2. Cookie with form feed is saved, see 0c byte before the 0a terminator
`````
curl -c cookies.txt http://127.0.0.1:3333
`````

summary: An attacker can poison curl's cookie store with cookies containing control characters like form feed, causing Apache to reject subsequent requests with a 400 Bad Request and leading to denial of service.

claims.text: curl does not implement character check on cookie name or value when saving to cookie store
claims.reasoning: The provided source code does not include the cookie parsing and storage logic (typically in lib/cookie.c). The snippets show only lib/urldata.h (CURLcode typedef) and lib/c-hyper.c (a function that calls Curl_http_cookies). The code that would validate or reject control characters when saving cookies is not present, so the claim cannot be verified from the provided code.
Same as C1: the cookie store implementation is not in the provided source snippets.

claims.text: a form feed character '\f' saved in cookie store
claims.reasoning: The trigger depends on the cookie parsing code accepting a form feed character, which is not in the provided source.

claims.text: Apache rejects control characters other than \r or \n in the request head, returning 400 Bad Request
claims.reasoning: This claim is about Apache HTTP server behavior, not curl code. The provided external source (E1) is an RFC 6265 erratum discussing cookie-octet syntax (excluding control characters per the spec), but it does not state that Apache rejects such characters in request headers. No excerpt confirms Apache's behavior.

key_reasons: The central claim (C1) is that curl lacks validation of control characters when saving cookies. The code that would confirm or contradict this (cookie parsing/storage in lib/cookie.c) is not included in the provided source snippets.
The provided source only shows lib/urldata.h and a small part of lib/c-hyper.c, neither of which contains the Set-Cookie parsing logic.
The RFC 6265 erratum (E1) confirms the spec excludes control characters from cookie-octet, but does not address Apache's behavior (C4).
A human reviewer needs to examine lib/cookie.c (or equivalent) at the target revision to see if cookie name/value validation exists.
